chapter: Hampton, New York and Lee's own band
title: Hampton as leader: jealousy and the Diggy Diggy Doo challenge
summary: Lee admits jealousy of Hamp, a drummer himself, and describes their closing number of trading fours.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Playing in Lionel Hampton's big band

blocks.x: How did you like working with Hamp's band?

I liked working with Hamp's band, but I got to tell you -- I ran into the same thing with myself, you know, because Hamp was a drummer, also, and he played vibes. I think I was very jealous of him, you know, being very candid about it. I'm sure that I was,,because the man really liked me, you know? He let me do anything. If we broadcasted and played 3 tunes on the air, I would sing 2 of them, you know, and he's trying to push me, you know, but as I said -- again -- sometimes it takes you a long time to grow up, you know, and you don't appreciate what people are trying to do for you in many instances, so we used to have a challenge

thing. Well, you know, I had a pretty good technique, and I played from hand to hand, you know -- I didn't start everything with my right hand, you know. And so I played solos -- whichever hand was there, I would start with the left or the right hand, you know. Now an unschooled drummer starts everything with his right hand, and so we had a challenge thing called "Diggy Diggy Doo", and Hamp had a little tom tom down in front, you know, and the man worked so hard, and he had me way up here where like Sonny Greer used to sit, and that was the closing number -- "Diggy Diggy Doo" --and we would take fours, you know.

And so he would be down front, and Hamp was really playing hard; playing his fours, and you know, turning it over to me for me to play my fours, you know? And so I had to answer everything that he played, you know, but he would say to me, "Why do you look so disgusted?" And I would say, "Because I'm tired of answering you!" You know? And he would explain to me, "Well, I'm the leader. You know. You got to answer me -- you can't make me look bad." And I wanted to lead; I wanted him to try to answer what I was playing, you know?

But I had come up in sessions and things, where you tried to cut one another, you know? But you have to throw that away, really, when you work with a band and that. But Hamp was -- I mean he was really a pleasure and really one of the nicest men I've ever known, really. Hamp was pretty

religious, too. He used to -- in those days, he used to always have his Bible. This was in '40 and '41, you know, and everybody would be on the bus and the train or wherever they would be -- and he would be over in the corner reading his Bible, you know.
